messages.author: 5c009c55dafaeed0
messages.subject: assumptions of open abundance model
parts:
Hi All,

I'm hoping to get some feedback on whether or not an open abundance model is appropriate for my data. We're trying to estimate density, and we have repeated counts from visual surveys of small mammals (ground squirrels and prairie dogs) along 1-km transects for three summers. In the first summer, we performed one survey, and in summers two and three we did two surveys per transect, each about a month apart. Does the population need to be closed within summers?  I think mortality is fairly high, and I can imagine that some of our sample has been eaten by the time we return for the second survey in a summer.   We also recorded the distance to each detection, so maybe distance sampling would be better? I think that the Chandler et al (2011) model accounts for temporary emigration, but not demographic factors, so I'm not sure it's appropriate here.

Any input would be appreciated!

Lucretia

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] assumptions of open abundance model
parts:
hi Lucretia,
 for this data set you should definitely use the distance data in my opinion.  you could great each sample as a new primary period over which temporary emigration could occur, or you could "stack" the data, treating each year or period as a new site and model time variables as site covariates.
 the gdistsamp() function in unmarked should work for this data set.  There is an application to point transect sampling by Sillett et al. which is right here:
http://www.esajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1890/11-1400.1?journalCode=ecap
 We also have some online stuff from the workshops on using the distance sampling functions (linked on the unmarked google site)
regards
andy

Hi Again,

I asked a question a while ago about how to analyze transect-based prey surveys that were repeated at the same locations 5 times over 3 years.  I ended up using gdistsamp but "stacking" the data, so treating each surveyXtransect as a new site and including the survey number as a site covariate (as was recommended when I first asked the question).  The density estimates seem reasonable, and now I'd like to create one predicted prey density 'surface' over my study area based on all survey periods.  Is this possible? What should I do with the survey number covariate when making predictions? Should I make predictions for each survey period and average them? Or maybe disregard the temporal survey covariate when making spatial predictions? My model output is below. 

Thanks for any suggestions! 
Lucretia

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] assumptions of open abundance model
parts:
All, 

I have used a similar approach to that described above, except using distsamp() as opposed to gdistsamp().  Specifically, we did point counts at ~200 sites distributed across three different wildfires that burned at different times.  To analyze, I stacked the data for each year yielding ~800 site x year combinations.  However, instead of including year as a site covariate, I used time since burn (in years).  I'm thinking it is functionally the same.

Anyway, my question:  Doesn't this approach treat site[i] in year one as independent from site[i] in year 2 or 3 or 4?  This is obviously not the case.  My p-values are super small and I'm wondering if this might be the reason.  output from a model included below.

Call:
distsamp(formula = ~1 ~ burnsev + I(burnsev^2) + tsb + tsb:burnsev + 
    prefire + slope + aspect + elevation, data = umf.fosp, keyfun = "halfnorm", 
    output = "density")

Density (log-scale):

4.13 0.0126 329       0

AIC: 7272.65 
Number of sites: 864
optim convergence code: 0
optim iterations: 129 
Bootstrap iterations: 0 

Thanks,
Paul
